n: At last the promise is fulfilled. The verse twice stresses that God did exactly what He said. Twenty-five years after the first promise, God keeps His word.

f.g: Came to bless; “visit” in scripture often means God’s active intervention.

n: Sarah becomes pregnant and bears a son to Abraham in their old age, right on God’s timetable.
Abraham names his son Isaac, as God instructed.
Abraham circumcises Isaac on the eighth day, faithfully keeping the covenant sign.
Abraham is a hundred years old—the birth is clearly a miracle.
Sarah’s laughter of doubt has become laughter of joy, and she invites everyone to share it.

f.w: God hath made me to laugh
f.g: Wordplay on Isaac’s name; her earlier laughter (18:12) is transformed.

n: Sarah marvels: who would have imagined she would nurse a baby? Her joyful poem celebrates the impossible made real.
Isaac is weaned—probably around age two or three—and Abraham celebrates with a feast, marking that the child had survived the dangerous early years.

f.g: Stopped nursing; in the ancient world often at two or three years old.

n: At the feast, Sarah sees Ishmael, now a teenager, mocking or playing. The word is again a wordplay on Isaac’s name. Paul later describes Ishmael as persecuting Isaac.

f.g: Hebrew metsaḥeq — laughing, playing, or mocking; from the same root as “Isaac.”

n: Sarah demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away so Ishmael will not share Isaac’s inheritance.

f.w: Cast out this bondwoman and her son

n: Abraham is deeply distressed. Ishmael is his son, and he loves him.
God reassures Abraham to follow Sarah’s counsel, because the covenant line will be traced through Isaac.

f.w: in Isaac shall thy seed be called

n: God promises that Ishmael, as Abraham’s son, will also become a nation. God has not forgotten him.
Early the next morning Abraham sends Hagar and Ishmael off with bread and water. They wander in the desert near Beersheba.

f.g: A waterskin made of animal hide.
A town at the northern edge of the Negev desert.

n: When the water runs out, Hagar places her son under a bush for shade, expecting him to die.
Hagar sits at a distance, unable to watch her son die, and weeps aloud. Her grief is one of scripture’s most heartrending scenes.

f.g: About the distance an arrow can fly.

n: God hears the boy’s cry—fitting for a child named “God hears.” The angel comforts Hagar with “fear not.”

f.w: God heard the voice of the lad
f.g: Fulfills the meaning of Ishmael’s name.

n: The angel tells Hagar to lift up her son, for God will make him a great nation.

f.g: Take him firmly by the hand.

n: God opens Hagar’s eyes to see a well. Often the help we need is near, but God must open our eyes to see it.
God is with Ishmael as he grows up in the desert and becomes a skilled archer.

f.g: God’s presence and blessing continue with Ishmael.

n: Ishmael settles in the wilderness of Paran, and Hagar finds him an Egyptian wife, from her own people.

f.g: A desert in the northeastern Sinai.

n: Abimelech and his army commander approach Abraham. Even outsiders recognize that God is with Abraham.

f.w: God is with thee in all that thou doest

n: Abimelech asks Abraham to swear a treaty of loyalty with him and his descendants, in return for the kindness he had shown.
Abraham agrees to swear.
Abraham complains that Abimelech’s servants seized one of his wells. In dry country, wells were precious and worth fighting over.
Abimelech says he knew nothing of it until now.
Abraham gives livestock, and the two make a covenant—a formal peace treaty.
Abraham sets apart seven female lambs.
Abimelech asks what the seven lambs mean.

f.g: What is the meaning of these?

n: By accepting the lambs, Abimelech publicly acknowledges that Abraham dug the well—a legal witness to ownership.

f.g: Evidence or proof of an agreement.

n: The place is called Beersheba, which can mean both “well of seven” and “well of the oath.”

f.g: Hebrew sheva means “seven”; nishbaʿ means “to swear an oath.”

n: After the treaty, Abimelech and Phichol return to Philistine territory.

f.g: The narrator uses the name familiar to later readers.

n: Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and worships the Lord as “the everlasting God.” A long-lived tree fits the eternal God and Abraham’s settling in the land.

f.g: Hebrew ’eshel — a tamarisk tree, a hardy desert tree.

n: Abraham lives for a long time in Philistine territory.
